Congress to Eliminate Billions in Wall Street Subsidies to Fund Repair of Nation's Highways

This is a highly simplified explanation of what's going on, and it puts me and some other economic moderates in the unenviable position of defending banks. Any bank that joins the Federal Reserve System must invest 6% of their assets into a kind of stock in the Fed. This stock cannot be traded, sold, or invested elsewhere, so because those funds are locked up, the Fed pays a dividend of 6% on the stocks to compensate the banks for joining the Federal Reserve System. This highway bill, which is necessary to fund the nation's infrastructure, cuts that dividend to 1.5% (because god forbid we raise the gas tax even the tiniest bit). If this rate proves too low for banks, they will stop joining the Fed and some may even withdraw, weakening the Fed's ability to regulate monetary policy in the U.S.

In other words, we are looking at a short-term cash grab by Congress, taking completely unrelated funds to repair our highways instead of raising the gas tax that was designed to pay for them. In the long run, this could be a serious problem for the Federal Reserve System, and we will see how things change in three years when we need more money for our roads.
